hero.name: Anil
hero.who: a 61-year-old retired bank manager in Mysuru who wants strong, independent later years

story.b: Anil retired from his bank last year after thirty-four years. He planned his money carefully: pension, savings, a small house in Mysuru with a garden. Now he is on the morning train to Bengaluru to visit his three-year-old granddaughter. He tries to lift his suitcase onto the overhead rack and cannot quite manage it. A college boy jumps up to help. At his daughter's flat, he sits on the floor to build a block tower with his granddaughter, and when he tries to stand, he has to grip the sofa and pull himself up. He laughs it off. On the train home, though, he thinks about it. He planned thirty years of money. He never planned his body.

ask.q: Anil feels fine but struggles with a suitcase and getting up from the floor. What is the wisest response?
o: Treat it as a signal to start planning his health for the decades ahead
Accept it as normal ageing that nothing can change
Wait until a real problem shows up before doing anything
ask.why: Small struggles now can be early signs worth acting on, and strength can often still be built in the sixties. Accepting it as fate, or waiting for a serious problem, gives up years when steady effort could help most. Planning ahead protects his independence.

chapters.take: Plan for a strong old age the way you plan for retirement money.

story.b: At home, Anil sits at his desk with the same diary he used for bank targets. At the top of a fresh page he writes: at eighty, I want to. Then he lists things. Lift my granddaughter. Carry my own bag onto a train. Climb the steps to Chamundi Hill with my old colleagues. Work in my garden for an hour. Travel alone to visit my sister in Pune. Getting up from the floor without help. He looks at the list and works backwards. All of it needs strong legs, good balance, enough stamina and a clear head. None of it will just happen. He realises that the old age he wants has to be built now, starting this year.

ask.q: Anil's friend says his only health goal is to live to ninety. What would make that goal more useful?
o: Focus on taking more vitamins to live longer
Avoid all effort so he saves energy for old age
Add what he wants to still do physically, like climbing stairs and travelling alone
ask.why: Living long is only half the goal, and what matters just as much is how well those years go. Vitamins alone are not a plan, and avoiding effort usually leaves people weaker. Naming the activities he wants to keep doing shows what to build now.

chapters.take: Aim for strong years, not just long ones. Picture what you want to do.

story.b: Anil has not had a health check in over two years. He felt fine, so it never seemed urgent. Now he books a routine check-up at a hospital near his house. A week later he sits with the doctor and the reports. His blood sugar is at the higher end, and his blood pressure is a little raised. Nothing alarming, the doctor says, but worth acting on now rather than later. She suggests some changes and asks him to come back in three months. Anil walks out into the sunshine feeling oddly grateful. If he had waited for symptoms, these numbers might have kept quietly climbing for years without him knowing.

ask.q: Anil's brother feels perfectly fine and says check-ups are only for sick people. What should Anil suggest?
o: Wait for symptoms, since tests often worry people for nothing
Get a routine check-up and discuss the results with a doctor
Order a big list of tests online and read the results himself
ask.why: Many common problems can build quietly for years before any symptom appears, so waiting can mean losing valuable time. Self-ordered tests without guidance can confuse or mislead. A routine check-up with a doctor can catch early signs and turn them into a sensible plan.

chapters.take: Do not wait for symptoms. Check early, with a doctor's guidance.

story.b: Anil asks his doctor about exercise, and she encourages him to start gently. So he begins with brisk morning walks around Kukkarahalli lake. He keeps a pace where he can still talk, but would not want to sing. Thirty minutes at first, then forty-five. After a month, he adds a few short uphill stretches near the university, where his breath gets heavy for a minute before easing. His old colleague Prakash joins him on Tuesdays and Fridays, and they argue about cricket the whole way round. Anil notices small things. He sleeps more soundly. The stairs to his terrace feel easier. He looks forward to the walk instead of dreading it.

ask.q: Anil's neighbour wants to start exercising after years of none. What is the best way to begin?
o: Check with his doctor, then start with brisk walks he can talk through, building up slowly
Join the hardest bootcamp in town to make up for lost time
Wait until he loses some weight before exercising at all
ask.why: Jumping into intense training after years off risks injury, and waiting for weight loss delays the very thing that can help most. Checking with his doctor and starting with steady, comfortable walks lets his body adapt, and harder efforts can be added later.

chapters.take: Steady movement, started gently and kept up, is one of the strongest health tools.

story.b: One day Anil hears that his neighbour, a man his own age, slipped in the bathroom and now needs help just to walk. It shakes him. Walking is good, but he knows his legs and balance need more. With his doctor's approval, he joins a twice-weekly strength class for older adults at a small gym nearby, with a careful trainer. They start light: sitting down and standing up from a chair, carrying weights, simple step-ups. At home he practises standing on one leg while brushing his teeth, holding the basin at first. He carries the vegetable bags back from Devaraja market himself. Every evening he practises getting up from the floor, using his hands less each week.

ask.q: Anil's wife thinks strength training is only for young people. What is the best reply?
o: Agree, and stick to walking only
Agree, since lifting anything at sixty is risky
Explain that strength and balance help people stay independent, and starting light with guidance is sensible
ask.why: Walking is great but does not do everything. Strength and balance tend to fade with age, and falls can be very serious for older people. Starting light, with a trainer and a doctor's advice, builds what keeps them independent instead of avoiding it out of fear.

chapters.take: Muscle and balance are savings for old age. Start depositing now.

story.b: Anil is walking and lifting well, yet some afternoons he feels low. The house is too quiet. He misses the bank, the colleagues, being useful. At first he ignores it and simply walks faster. Then he admits to his wife that he feels lonely, and she suggests he talk to their family doctor too. He makes a few changes. He keeps a fixed bedtime and charges his phone in the hall. With his doctor's advice, he adds more dal, curd and sprouts to his meals and eats smaller portions of rice. He joins his walking friends for filter coffee after the lake. And twice a week he teaches maths to children at a nearby government school.

ask.q: Anil is eating and exercising well but feels low and lonely since retiring. What should he do?
o: Ignore it, since physical health is what really counts
Treat it as part of his health, reconnecting with people and talking to someone if it lasts
Exercise harder so he is too tired to feel low
ask.why: Emotional health matters as much as the physical kind, so ignoring it leaves half the picture out. Exercising harder to numb feelings does not address them. Reconnecting with people, and speaking to a doctor or counsellor if low moods last, cares for the whole person.

chapters.take: Food, sleep and a contented mind matter as much as exercise.

story.h: The same train, six months on
story.b: Six months later, Anil takes the same morning train to Bengaluru. This time he lifts his suitcase onto the rack himself, a little slowly, but without help. At his daughter's flat, his granddaughter drags him to the floor to play, and when it is time for lunch, he gets up without reaching for the sofa. She claps, thinking it is a trick. His follow-up check showed his numbers moving in a better direction, and his doctor was pleased. He still walks at Kukkarahalli with Prakash, still argues about cricket, still teaches maths on Tuesdays. His diary list for eighty is pinned above his desk. He reads it most mornings before putting on his walking shoes.

chapters.take: Small, steady care today can buy strong, independent years tomorrow.
